consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same primary symbolic identification: fornication/whoredom, when used figuratively, signifies spiritual unfaithfulness to God — chiefly idolatry and apostasy — grounded in the covenant-as-marriage metaphor, with Israel/Jerusalem/Babylon personified as an unfaithful wife or harlot. Recognized subsidiary applications include illicit political/commercial alliances with foreign powers, corrupt or apostate religious systems, and general worldliness; the plain literal sense of sexual immorality coexists in ethical texts.
book_summary: The book defines fornication/whoredom as spiritual unfaithfulness — breaking covenant with God to go after other gods and kingdoms — emphasizing that the symbol is not merely the physical sin: the out-of-covenant union itself constitutes the whoredom.
consensus_core_identification: Symbolic fornication/whoredom = covenant unfaithfulness to God, principally idolatry/apostasy (with political alliance with foreign powers as a closely related extension), under the marriage metaphor between God and His people.
book_core_identification: Fornication/whoredom = spiritual unfaithfulness, i.e., covenant-breaking pursuit of other gods and kingdoms; the out-of-covenant union itself is the whoredom, not merely the physical act.
boundary_disagreement: None of substance. The book's phrase 'and kingdoms' explicitly folds political alliance into the primary definition, whereas some consensus responses list it as a secondary application; but Responses A, C, and D all acknowledge political entanglement as part of the same unfaithfulness motif, so this is emphasis rather than a boundary shift. The book's 'not merely the physical sin' aligns with the consensus view that the literal sexual sense is distinct from the symbolic use.
material_contradiction: None. Both readings identify the same referent (covenant unfaithfulness/idolatry under the marriage metaphor) in the same sense.
rationale: Reduced to minimum cores, the book and consensus say the same thing: whoredom symbolizes spiritual unfaithfulness to God through pursuit of other gods (idolatry) and worldly powers, rooted in the covenant/marriage framework. The book's inclusion of 'kingdoms' matches the widely acknowledged political-alliance dimension (Ezekiel 16/23, Isaiah 23, Revelation 17–18), and its 'out-of-covenant union is itself the whoredom' formulation is a wording-level nuance of the same identification, not a change of extension. No cases are added, excluded, or reclassified relative to the consensus.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book's formulation 'the out-of-covenant union is itself the whoredom' subtly broadens the symbol to make any non-covenantal alliance (religious, political, or marital, per Ex 34:16 and the cross-reference to Marriage and Divorce) constitutive of whoredom, which might push toward REFINED as a slight broadening beyond idolatry proper. But since the consensus responses already include political alliance and worldly entanglement within the same motif, this reading does not materially alter the extension.
